narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 91.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to assess risk, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by your academic performance during law school itself. Your first-year and third-year class rankings were the two strongest factors pushing the model toward a failure prediction. Both placed you at the very bottom of your class (decile 1), far below the average of accepted students who typically ranked around the middle of their class (decile 6 and 5.8 respectively). These unusually low rankings strongly signaled to the model that you would struggle with the bar exam.

Your LSAT score was the third most important factor, but it worked in the opposite direction. At 37, your score sits almost exactly at the average of students who were accepted, which slightly pulled the prediction toward success. Unfortunately, this positive influence was not nearly enough to overcome the much stronger negative signals from your class rankings.

Given these results, you should focus on improving your academic performance if you retake courses or consider a different admissions cycle. Strengthening your class standing would likely have the biggest impact on future predictions. You may also want to explore schools or programs that place less weight on bar passage predictions or provide additional academic support.
